title: E30 - Is AI Disrupting ALSPs? Axiom CSO Catherine Kemnitz
author: Catherine Kemnitz

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source does not endorse the claimed competence crisis or loss of apprenticeship work. Instead, it reframes generative AI as a potentially interactive training aid that could explain senior feedback and improve on static resources. These benefits are hypothetical and experience-based, not measured outcomes or a developed replacement-apprenticeship model.
qs: I mean, I think today, like what I would do with like a a hand markup from an attorney that I could barely read and didn't really understand, I think I could probably do wonders having ChatGPT just to walk me through the senior attorney's hand markup.
So I think there was so much today from a training perspective that you can do, that you just couldn't do then where PLC was, like you said, sort of this like static version of training.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source addresses enterprise legal-department experimentation and attributes some uptake to company-wide AI licenses. It does not assess whether AI can expand meaningful legal help or whether adoption alone can close the justice gap, so its evidence is relevant only to the cluster’s ancillary adoption discussion.
qs: The other thing is, in many instances, I actually see legal departments outpacing law firms on AI adoption, which I wouldn't have guessed.
But the reason that I've seen that happen is legal departments very often have access to either ChatGPT, Google Gemini or Claude by virtue of a company wide license program.

st.t: Contract infrastructure: AI challenges siloed CLM systems
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s view that AI exposes pre-existing CLM weaknesses while leaving the viability of AI-first rebuilding unresolved. It materially extends the argument beyond contract software to ALSPs and other talent-based legal-service providers, contending that changing client expectations require service redesign even without inevitable automation.
qs: I certainly could imagine that the CLM is disruptible because I think it had problems even before AI came along.

I think we are in very much like in the crosshairs and need to adapt not because we're going to be automated out of a job, but just because the standards in general and the expectations of what people want is changing so rapidly.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim that in-house AI adoption can shift capacity-driven work and spending away from law firms while preserving demand for sophisticated external advice. It materially extends that proposition by describing an ALSP delivery model in which Axiom uses its own vetted technology stack to perform work and demonstrate tools when clients face procurement or implementation barriers.
qs: And part of it, I think, ties to the desire for in-house to sort of move the flow of spend from law firms to doing things themselves.

Now in terms of the actual tech, this kind of too general path, in order to do it the way we do it right now for larger projects, we have to use our own tech stack unless the client already has the solution.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Kemnitz accepts the cluster’s core view that AI will restructure legal-service production rather than eliminate lawyers. She materially extends it with a concrete allocation model: in-house teams absorb smaller routine matters, law firms retain sophisticated advice, and ALSPs deliver high-volume work through human-plus-technology workflows requiring calibration, validation and client supervision.
qs: And part of it, I think, ties to the desire for in-house to sort of move the flow of spend from law firms to doing things themselves.

If it's 50,000, I do want somebody with true technological knowledge and ability to kind of calibrate the tech, make sure all the cell queries are right, make sure we test and validate along the way to be with us.

st.t: Vendor strategy: Faster building cannot eliminate integration
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s emphasis on adoption as a people-dependent, staged process and materially extends its vendor-strategy analysis by arguing that AI may disrupt an already-troubled CLM category, while remaining uncertain that an AI-first rebuild will succeed. These are strategic opinions rather than measured evidence.
qs: But, again, because we were back to being people first, the way we had to engage needed to see where the tech was landing a little bit.
I'm not 100% sure that as products, that the CLM is able to be rebuilt quote unquote, AI first, which I think is a separate topic.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Axiom accepts the cluster’s core view that AI will redesign rather than wholesale replace legal work, with humans continuing to use technology and check outputs. It materially extends the proposition through an ALSP operating model built around client-calibrated workflows, vetted technology, transparent savings and flexible pricing or engagement structures.
qs: And we continue to believe that for the foreseeable future, certainly, but maybe forever, whatever technology we use, especially in illegal matters, will require some level of humans who first know how to use it, but also can make sure that once you get that output, because when everybody has the tech, somebody's going to have to have a competitive edge over that.
We want to be bending with it and learning from clients, and more importantly, serving clients so that while they do this, we are with them.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: Kemnitz supports the cluster’s proposition that corporate legal departments are becoming central to AI-driven change: their strategic importance is rising while executive demands for AI-enabled savings are removing legal’s traditional exemption from technology adoption. Her account also reinforces organisational readiness as a constraint through legal’s technology immaturity, but provides qualitative expectations rather than measured savings or implementation outcomes.
qs: It's the CEO saying, all of you guys, whether you're marketing, legal, you name it, need to find those savings and use AI to do it because that's going to be true across the board.
I think part of why legal can sometimes feel like a low-hanging fruit, it's its technology immaturity.

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: Kemnitz directly supports the cluster’s user-led adoption proposition: owning legal-tech tools does not ensure use, so firms should begin with concrete, burdensome tasks lawyers want completed faster. Her support is practical but anecdotal and does not demonstrate measured adoption outcomes.
qs: And you're like, well, have you asked them stuff they hate doing that takes time and try to map that to a use case?
I was like, well, trust me, if you do something they hate doing fast, they're going to want to use the tech.

st.t: Contract intelligence: Business coordination exceeds document storage
st.an: The source broadly supports the synthesis by treating AI adoption as an operational and organisational issue rather than a document-storage question. It reinforces the cluster’s conclusions on enterprise-vetting barriers, technology-enabled internal capacity, continued demand for sophisticated outside advice, and uncertainty over whether generic or specialist tools will prevail. It adds relevant implementation evidence but does not materially extend the central contract-intelligence proposition.
qs: Part of the benefit of what we do sometimes is it can be really hard for a large enterprise to get technology vetted internally to be adopted by the in-house department.
And I'm not sure where it's probably going to be a bit of both, and maybe we have multiple tools for different things.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source supports redesigning legal-service delivery around AI-enabled client needs while retaining human expertise, validation and accountability. It also aligns with the cluster’s view that in-house adoption may reallocate work, pricing and engagement models may evolve, and current market effects remain strategic judgments rather than measured outcomes.
qs: If it's 50,000, I do want somebody with true technological knowledge and ability to kind of calibrate the tech, make sure all the cell queries are right, make sure we test and validate along the way to be with us.

And going back to the innovation solution, it's always go after the clients that are not served well, the business model innovation, and kind of roll with it versus being sort of stuck in your way and saying, I hope we hold that wall as long as possible.

st.t: Legal leadership: Business capability complements legal expertise
st.an: Kemnitz’s account supports the proposition that operational and strategic capability can complement legal expertise and create a cross-functional route into leadership. Her move from predominantly legal responsibilities into strategy, alongside Axiom’s investment in operational readiness and a dedicated career GC, illustrates role specialisation rather than a universal career formula.
qs: And so started working on really public company readiness, operations and so on.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s broader claims that generative AI will materially expand and transform legal work and that in-house adoption may benefit from organisational access to general-purpose tools. It does not, however, substantively address the cluster’s central thesis that specialist workflow layers and verified copilot architectures will defend durable value.
qs: And I think in part because, and you can come back to this, I think the tech that even though you're still going to have some of the reflexes of the legal industry, legal will not be able to insulate itself from this transformation in the way that it has in the past.
But the reason that I've seen that happen is legal departments very often have access to either ChatGPT, Google Gemini or Claude by virtue of a company wide license program.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s view that legal AI requires business-model and service adaptation rather than technology acquisition alone. It reinforces client-led redesign, continued human oversight and experimentation, while treating future pricing and delivery models as unsettled predictions rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: You have to be willing to say, we might have to suffer that shift and repivot on the technology usage side as a business model.
We want to be bending with it and learning from clients, and more importantly, serving clients so that while they do this, we are with them.

st.t: Vendor value: Concentration forecasts face diverse competition
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of AI-first service delivery as a competitive challenge distinct from software-vendor competition. It specifically raises possible disruption of incumbent ALSPs such as Axiom, while offering only a hypothesis and discussion agenda—not evidence of actual displacement or an incumbent response.
qs: Katherine and I got into a little spat on LinkedIn because someone from Axiom had posted about the fact that CLM was going to be disrupted by AI, and I argued, well, ALSPs, like Axiom, alternative legal service providers, may be disrupted as well.
We got into an entire conversation on the podcast about how incumbents and how incumbent ALSPs in particular plan to respond to the AI disruption.

kp.k: ALSP incumbents face disruption alongside traditional law firms
kp.d: Kemnitz explicitly agrees with Abramowitz that Axiom is vulnerable to AI disruption, describing it as both a disruptor and an incumbent. Her reference to losing half the business in two years is a strategic stress scenario, not a forecast. She advocates self-cannibalisation through tested technology and trained lawyers rather than defending existing delivery methods; hypothetical competitors offering dramatically faster, cheaper services motivate that position.
qs: We are immensely at risk.
what if this wiped out half of business in two years?
And we're equally an incumbent to be disrupted by those who might do what we do better.
if somebody is going to cannibalize us, it should be ourselves.

kp.k: Professional services must adapt to changing client expectations
kp.d: Abramowitz frames disruption as broader than job automation: changing standards and expectations require talent-based professional services businesses, including his own, to reconsider their offerings. Separately, he argues that contract lifecycle management was troubled before AI and remains disruptible, while expressing uncertainty about whether its products can be rebuilt AI-first. These are the host's assessments, not demonstrated market findings.
qs: any business, especially one in professional services, especially ones that are built on human talent, we like are not immune.
need to adapt not because we're going to be automated out of a job, but just because the standards in general and the expectations of what people want is changing so rapidly.
I certainly could imagine that the CLM is disruptible because I think it had problems even before AI came along.

kp.k: Axiom's earlier restructuring anticipated technology-driven disruption
kp.d: Kemnitz connects Axiom's 2019 technology spin-offs and concentration on talent to a strategic belief that technology would evolve but Axiom should not build it itself or double down on its most disruptible activities. She also argues that technology, managed services and talent businesses require different economics and sales capabilities. She reports focused generative-AI attention beginning approximately two and a half years before the interview, with leadership strategy sessions preceding more aggressive engagement.
qs: We do think we're not the ones who are going to build it.
If you remember even in 2019 when we had technology, we spun that off.
You need very separate kind of skill set to sell different things.
I think the Gen.A.I. piece probably, I want to say two and a half years ago, is when we were like, okay, now we're paying attention.

kp.k: AI could turn legal content into personalised transactional workflows
kp.d: Drawing on Practical Law's content model, Kemnitz envisages generative AI converting static practice guidance and forms into interactive assistance, including an IPO process with documents drafted from a firm's precedents or a company's data. This is a statement of technological potential, not a report of a deployed product or measured performance.
qs: this associate with all the content that's truly interactive
not just say, here's what you need to do in an IPO, but here's your IPO process.
not pre-drafted as a static form, pre-drafted from your precedent or your company's data.

kp.k: Axiom promises transparent delivery and client efficiency savings
kp.d: Kemnitz positions Axiom's AI-assisted model as an extension of in-house departments: clients would pay for fewer human hours, see the technology vetted by Axiom and have visibility into the work. She presents passing savings through to clients as a distinction from law firms. The transcript supplies no quantified realised savings or comparison study, and she emphasises variation among businesses grouped under the ALSP label.
qs: You get the savings because, well, you're going to pay less human hours than you would otherwise.
you're going to have visibility into the tech we've vetted.
This is not behind a curtain because we continue to be an extension of the in-house department.

kp.k: Generative AI redirected investment away from Arizona legal practice
kp.d: Kemnitz reports that Axiom closed its Arizona Advice and Counsel operation, which regulatory changes had enabled it to establish to provide legal advice. She says the operation performed well but competing innovation priorities and resource requirements led Axiom to favour generative AI's potential. This is an account of a company resource-allocation decision, not a claim that regulation required closure.
qs: We actually shut that down.
The re-regulation there really got us very excited about starting law firm and basically allowed us to take the extra step towards like, can we give the legal advice?
look where GenAI can take us versus what we're going to be able to do just with that structure and all the resource allocation that it required made that choice quite important to do.

kp.k: Client supervision and technology environments shape AI service delivery
kp.d: Kemnitz explains that clients supervise Axiom's lawyers and must help calibrate AI-assisted contract reviews rather than receive an independent Axiom legal opinion. Larger projects currently use Axiom's technology stack unless clients already have the solution. She reports about half of Axiom's lawyers work in client environments and describes Axiom laptops and tools as a way clients can experience outputs before potentially adopting software internally.
qs: we're going to really work with a client to kind of calibrate how the review is done. They have to be involved in that.
for larger projects, we have to use our own tech stack unless the client already has the solution.
But they are fine if a lawyer, for instance, use our laptops, they have then the tech on there.
I would say about half of them are in client environment

kp.k: Executive mandates weaken legal departments' claims to technological exceptionalism
kp.d: Kemnitz considers generative AI categorically different from earlier legal technology because its wider societal and business adoption prevents legal from insulating itself. She argues that CEOs are mandating AI savings across functions and that legal's technological immaturity can make it appear an attractive starting point. She also describes a strengthened strategic role for in-house counsel as rapidly changing risks and regulations demand timely business guidance.
qs: legal will not be able to insulate itself from this transformation in the way that it has in the past.
It's the CEO saying, all of you guys, whether you're marketing, legal, you name it, need to find those savings and use AI to do it because that's going to be true across the board.
I think part of why legal can sometimes feel like a low-hanging fruit, it's its technology immaturity.
In-house has to move fast and be on the ball to really help guide the company.

kp.k: Generic AI adoption complicates legal-specific vendors' future
kp.d: Abramowitz reports observing some legal departments outpace law firms through company-wide access to generic AI products. Kemnitz agrees and says Axiom's data indicate substantial adoption of generic rather than legal-specific solutions, but provides no sample, figures or methodology. Looking two years ahead, she leaves open whether departments will upgrade to specialist tools or generic models will become sufficient with training and supervision, possibly producing a mixed-tool landscape.
qs: in many instances, I actually see legal departments outpacing law firms on AI adoption
Our data shows that, to your point, a lot of them are adopting generic solutions, not legal specific solutions.
what will actually adoption look like in legal two years from now?
Or will the generics become good enough in legal matters that with the right training and supervision, the legal tech feels like just a skin over that?

kp.k: AI may shift capacity-driven external spending into in-house ecosystems
kp.d: Kemnitz distinguishes work sent to law firms for sophisticated advice and assurance from work outsourced because internal teams lack capacity. She sees AI creating an opportunity to retain the latter, including surveys and document reviews, within in-house teams and their extensions. Her illustrative contrast between 100 and 50,000 documents explains Axiom's proposed role: supplying lawyers and technological expertise to configure, test and validate larger-scale work, rather than merely supplying software.
qs: But then there's all the stuff you just sent to law firms because you don't have time and capacity.
In-house is in-house and it's extensions.
if it's 100 docs, I can run it through AI myself. If it's 50,000, I do want somebody with true technological knowledge and ability to kind of calibrate the tech
So we want the lawyers, the humans with the tech, that's where we come in.

kp.k: Changing human-machine shares may require new business models
kp.d: Kemnitz uses an illustrative shift from 80% human work and 20% technology to the reverse over a couple of years to explain why Axiom needs flexibility. She expects humans to remain necessary for the foreseeable future, possibly indefinitely, both to use technology and contribute creativity beyond model content. She anticipates possible new pricing and engagement models but specifies neither a settled replacement model nor observed labour displacement.
qs: something today may be 80% done by a human, 20 per tech. And maybe that evolves in a couple of years. It's the reverse.
for the foreseeable future, certainly, but maybe forever
that's going to come from the invention and the creativity, I think, of the stuff that's not yet into the language models.
It may mean new pricing models.

kp.k: AI offers potential informal training support for junior lawyers
kp.d: Abramowitz reflects that generative AI could have helped him learn while practising as a junior lawyer around 2010–2013, especially in a culture discouraging questions to senior attorneys. He suggests using ChatGPT to decipher and explain senior lawyers' handwritten amendments, contrasting this interactive support with static Practical Law materials. This is a retrospective hypothetical, not evidence of improved training outcomes.
qs: there's a kind of culture of don't ask the senior attorney, figure it out on your own.
I think I could probably do wonders having ChatGPT just to walk me through the senior attorney's hand markup.
PLC was, like you said, sort of this like static version of training.

kp.k: Safe experimentation builds adoption skills and verification habits
kp.d: Both speakers recommend hands-on use before attempting broader redesign. Kemnitz suggests giving two or three enthusiastic department members a month to experiment in a secure sandbox, beginning with disliked, time-consuming tasks. Her anecdote about repeatedly correcting an AI-generated image illustrates why users need repeated practice to recognise shortcomings in outputs, including contracts. She applies the same use-case-first advice to law firms struggling to get associates to use purchased tools.
qs: maybe you find two or three people in your department super excited and say, you have a month to go play.
You can build enough of a playground, a sandbox, whatever, to preserve your security and all of that.
I'm going to have to build that muscle to really identify where it's still coming short. That takes reps, lots and lots of reps.
if you do something they hate doing fast, they're going to want to use the tech.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Catherine Kemnitz presents generative AI as a categorical transformation that threatens incumbent ALSPs while creating opportunities for technology-enabled service delivery.
pts.d: Kemnitz argues that legal cannot shield itself from this transformation as it has from previous technologies. Axiom is both a disruptor of traditional legal delivery and an incumbent vulnerable to competitors. Her response is self-cannibalisation: test technology, train lawyers and offer clients a less human-hour-intensive alternative. The possibility of losing half the business in two years is a strategic stress-test scenario, not a forecast. She also reports that Axiom closed its Arizona advice-and-counsel operation because pursuing generative AI opportunities took priority in innovation resource allocation; she does not describe the closure as evidence that AI had automated that operation.

pts.k: Kemnitz predicts that generative AI could turn authoritative but static legal content into interactive, context-specific workflow and drafting assistance.
pts.d: Using Practical Law as her example, Kemnitz envisages moving from practice notes and forms to an interactive associate-like resource that supplies an IPO process and drafts using a firm's precedents or a company's data. This is a potential capability grounded in the combination of content and technology, rather than a reported deployment or measured result.

pts.k: Kemnitz anticipates AI-enabled insourcing of capacity-driven law-firm work, with ALSPs supplying technology-capable lawyers for larger projects.
pts.d: She distinguishes work sent to law firms for sophisticated advice and assurance from work outsourced because legal departments lack time or capacity. AI could enable departments and their external extensions, including Axiom, to retain more of the second category. Larger document projects would still create demand for people who configure tools, test and validate their operation, and work with clients. She leaves open whether departments will graduate from generic AI to legal-specific products or whether generic models will become sufficiently capable with appropriate training and supervision.

pts.k: Kemnitz expects a changing human–technology division of labour, rather than the disappearance of people, potentially requiring new pricing and engagement models.
pts.d: Her illustrative scenario reverses a task mix from predominantly human to predominantly technological over a couple of years. She nevertheless expects a continuing need for humans who can operate technology and exercise judgement about its output. When technology becomes widely available, she locates competitive differentiation in human invention and creativity. These are strategic expectations, not measured productivity or staffing forecasts.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Kemnitz relies primarily on executive experience, Axiom's strategic decisions and client observations, with an unspecified reference to adoption data.
pts.d: Her evidence includes her involvement in the Practical Law acquisition, Axiom's 2019 decision to focus on people rather than build technology, leadership strategy sessions devoted to generative AI, and the closure of the Arizona operation. She says Axiom's data indicate faster in-house adoption and substantial use of generic rather than legal-specific tools, but supplies no figures, sample, methodology or measurement period. No model benchmarks, quantified service outcomes or measured client savings are offered. The document-volume and human–technology percentages are illustrative scenarios, not empirical findings.

pts.k: Her claims about adoption and checking output are supported by practitioner anecdotes and an analogy, not formal evaluation.
pts.d: Kemnitz recounts law firms asking how to get associates to use tools they already have. She proposes beginning with disliked, time-consuming tasks and building practical familiarity through repeated use. A personal image-generation anecdote, involving successive corrections that introduce or leave errors, illustrates why users must learn to identify shortcomings before relying on outputs in contracts. It is not a legal accuracy test or a measured hallucination rate.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Kemnitz combines current observations with explicitly uncertain one- to two-year scenarios and a longer-term expectation of continuing human involvement.
pts.d: In this 2025 source, she says focused attention to generative AI began roughly two and a half years earlier. She frames a two-year loss of half the business as a risk-management question, asks what legal adoption might look like two years ahead, and expects to watch the in-house ecosystem shift over the next year. Her possible reversal of human and technology shares occurs over a couple of years. She does not select a definitive generic-versus-specialist tool outcome and qualifies the duration of human involvement as the foreseeable future, possibly forever.

pts.k: Her service-delivery claims depend on client supervision, technology access, calibration, verification and secure experimentation.
pts.d: Kemnitz explains that Axiom's lawyers work under client supervision and that clients must participate in calibrating reviews, rather than Axiom independently providing a legal opinion through its staffing model. Large projects generally use Axiom's technology stack unless the client already has the solution; deployment also depends on whether lawyers work in Axiom's or the client's environment. Her document-volume example distinguishes manageable self-service from work requiring specialist technological support and testing. Successful adoption requires a secure setting and repeated practice identifying output shortcomings.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are corporate legal departments, incumbent ALSPs, traditional law firms and lawyers using AI.
pts.d: Corporate legal departments face executive pressure to obtain AI savings but may gain capacity, faster delivery and lower external spending. Axiom and comparable people-centred ALSPs face cannibalisation of human hours while seeking demand for technology-enabled extensions of in-house teams. Traditional law firms could lose capacity-driven assignments while retaining sophisticated advice work. Lawyers need practical tool skills, the ability to check outputs and creative differentiation. Legal-specific vendors face an uncertain competitive relationship with generic models. The discussion concerns enterprise legal delivery, not evidence of improved access to justice for underserved individuals.
